newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels sought American Berenson's release.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels sought American Berenson's release.

text.p: Peruvian rebels who held 72 hostages for four months had demanded freedom for U.S. citizen Lori Berenson as a way of winning over American public opinion, a newspaper said on Sunday.

Before a military raid ended the 126-day siege, the Tupac Amaru guerrillas had reduced their demands to freedom for 20 jailed comrades, including the group's leaders and Berenson, papers reported. They had originally sought freedom for 450 imprisoned rebels.

The 20 jailed rebels whose freedom they demanded in the last days of negotiations included Berenson and three Chileans in Peruvian jails, Jaime Castillo, Lautaro Mellado and Alejandro Astorga, the reports said.

Citing a hostage source, the newspaper Expreso said Berenson, a New Yorker sentenced to life imprisonment in 1995 for involvement in a Tupac Amaru bombing plot, was specifically included in the list as a way of swaying U.S. public opinion to support the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA).
The Clinton administration has repeatedly called for a non-military trial for Berenson, a 28-year-old with a history of social activism in Central America before she moved to Peru in the early 1990s.

The siege of the Japanese diplomatic compound ended last Tuesday when commandos swarmed into the house through secret tunnels, overwhelming the MRTA captors and rescuing all but one of the 72 hostages.
One hostage, two commandos and all 14 guerrillas died in the raid, which followed months of fruitless negotiations.
MRTA commander Nestor Cerpa grew over-confident in the last days of negotiations and was convinced that he was about to win the release of some of his jailed comrades, the daily La Republica said.

"Cerpa said that he had won the upper hand over the government," La Republica quoted a source close to negotiations as saying. "He was saying that everything would turn out all right and that there would be no deaths."
Cerpa's bullet-ridden corpse was later seen sprawled on a staircase in television footage of the gutted and bombed-out house, next to those of two other dead guerrillas.

Another source quoted in La Republica said Cerpa's personality seemed to change in the days before the raid, that he seemed filled with "enthusiasm, hope and illusions" and that he was deluded into thinking he would win a peaceful solution.
"He wasn't the same calculating, pessimistic man any more. He believed he could win, not right away, but soon," said the source, referring to Cerpa.
